planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, humusy soil in shade; its erect rhizomes are clothed in dark, almost black scales that make it easy to tell from similar Dryopteris.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich woodland soil in shade, where this Japanese and Chinese species forms an upright evergreen clump of once-pinnate, lance-shaped fronds whose lower leaflets curve forward in a distinctive way. It is sometimes mistaken in the garden for a slim-leaved Polystichum rather than a typical Dryopteris. Groom out tired fronds in late winter before the new crosiers push up, and leave it undisturbed once established, since it increases slowly from a single crown.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade; this vigorous Japanese species pushes up red-tinted new growth much like the related autumn fern.

directions: This East Asian wood fern arose naturally as an apogamous hybrid, which is part of why it increases so reliably from a single clone without needing a mate. Its arching, bipinnate fronds are leathery and broadly oval, emerging a striking brick-red in spring before settling into glossy mid-green by summer. Plant divisions in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade, where it builds into a vigorous three-foot-wide clump faster than most comparable wood ferns. It holds its evergreen fronds well through moderate winters and asks for little beyond an annual tidy-up of old growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, compost-laden soil in shade; this Himalayan species has proven surprisingly heat tolerant for a plant from cool, high-elevation valleys.

directions: True to its name, this Himalayan wood fern carries the most finely cut, airily textured fronds of any Dryopteris in general cultivation, giving it a soft, lacy look closer to a fine-leaved Dryopteris marginalis than a typical wood fern. It forms an upright, vase-shaped evergreen clump from rich valley soil at 5,000 to 7,000 feet in its native range, yet trial plantings as far south as central Texas show it tolerates far more summer heat than its origin would suggest. Grow it in moist, fertile, compost-rich soil in shade, and expect both deer and rabbits to leave it alone. Divide crowded clumps only occasionally, as it is a slow, well-mannered spreader.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, well-drained soil in light shade; despite a wide natural range from India to Taiwan, this species is still rarely seen in gardens.

directions: Native along watercourses from the Himalayan foothills east to Taiwan, this wood fern forms a solitary rosette of glossy, pleasantly ruffled evergreen fronds clothed in unusually pale scales. It has proven remarkably adaptable in cultivation given how specific its wild habitat sounds, tolerating a range of soil moisture once established. Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in light shade, and site it where its ruffled texture and pale, glossy foliage can stand out against plainer-leaved neighbors. It is largely untroubled by deer and rabbits.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, slightly moist organic soil in shade; collected at nearly 8,000 feet in Taiwan's Hualien County, it dies back in winter but regrows into an outsized clump each year.

directions: Collected on a high-elevation Taiwanese expedition, this is the largest and showiest selection of the genus Pteris grown outdoors, throwing up bizarrely branched, finger-like fronds on a scale that looks tropical even though the species dies to the ground each winter. Thick spreading rhizomes let a single plant expand into a wide, dramatic clump within a few seasons, so give it ample room away from smaller companions. Fertile fronds rise like a flagpole from the clump's center in early fall, adding an odd, architectural accent. It grows markedly faster and lusher in rich, moist, organic soil than in lean or dry sites, though it tolerates both.

planting.note: Wedge divisions into sharply drained, gritty soil pockets among rock in spring; a dryland fern from the desert Southwest that tolerates far more sun than most ferns.

directions: A tough little dryland fern of the southwestern United States, this species forms a tight, slowly spreading colony of fine, grayish evergreen fronds suited to rock gardens and troughs rather than a conventional shade bed. It handles far more direct sun than most ferns, provided drainage is sharp, though in the hottest climates it appreciates a few hours of afternoon shade to keep from scorching. Plant it among rocks or gravel in lean, fast-draining soil, and let it go dry between waterings once established, since soggy roots are its main vulnerability. It is also sold under the newer name Myriopteris wootonii.

planting.note: Wedge divisions into thin, gritty soil pockets among rock in part sun in spring; sharp drainage matters far more than soil fertility for this high-desert fern.

directions: Found naturally on rocky slopes and ledges, often beneath pines, from Colorado and Texas west into Arizona and northern Mexico, this lip fern spreads slowly from a creeping rhizome into a low tuft of finely, three-times-divided fronds. It survives mountain winters that would damage softer ferns, going semi-dormant in the driest part of summer and flushing fresh growth after rain. Tuck divisions into gritty, rocky soil pockets in a sunny to partly shaded rock garden, and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which shortens its life. It is now also classified as Myriopteris fendleri in current taxonomy.

planting.note: Plant divisions among rock or gravel in spring in sun to part sun with sharp drainage; keep this Australian native on the dry side through winter for best results.

directions: An Australian and New Zealand rock-crevice fern, this species forms a tight clump of stiff, dark stipes carrying crinkled, bristly-haired fronds that are rusty brown underneath and woolly white on top. It thrives on neglect in open, rocky, sun-exposed ground and is one of the more sun-tolerant plants of its genus. The single biggest key to success is keeping it dry through the cool season, since wet winter crowns are its main cause of failure. Use it in rockeries, troughs, or along a gravel path edge where its wiry, textured clumps read as a miniature accent.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into lean, sharply drained rock-crevice soil in part shade in spring, keeping the root zone cool; this western mountain species dislikes rich garden beds.

directions: This small western North American fern produces two distinct frond types from the same tuft: flat, lobed sterile fronds that genuinely resemble garden parsley, and narrower, curled fertile fronds that carry the spores on their undersides. It is a true rock dweller, rooting into cracks and crevices across coastal ranges and the Rockies, and old fronds from the previous year often persist at the base well into the next growing season. Plant divisions into lean, gritty, sharply drained crevice soil in part shade, keeping roots cool and avoiding rich, waterlogged beds. It makes an unusual, textural addition to an alpine trough or scree garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in part sun to light shade; its new fronds emerge pink-red before maturing to green.

directions: Named for the coarse, sandpapery feel of its narrow, toothed fronds, this Australian and Pacific evergreen puts out a flush of vivid red to pink new growth each spring that slowly ages to a darker green, giving it a long season of color contrast. Its once-pinnate fronds have a distinctly rough, finely serrated edge unlike the soft texture of most garden ferns. Grow it in evenly moist, humus-rich, mildly acidic soil in part sun to light shade, mulching heavily and wrapping with fleece during hard cold snaps at the edge of its hardiness range. Cut away old, faded fronds only once fresh new growth has started to emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, alkaline, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; it grows naturally in limestone rock pockets of Texas and Mexico.

directions: Native to limestone country across the Edwards Plateau, Trans-Pecos, and much of Mexico, this unusual fern earns its common name from upright, narrow fertile fronds that rise above the foliage and are easily mistaken for actual flowers. Its sterile fronds tolerate drought by curling inward when conditions turn dry, then relaxing back into shape once moisture returns. Plant it in gritty, alkaline, never-waterlogged soil in a well-drained rockery or slope in part sun to light shade. It is still rarely offered commercially, making it a genuine novelty for collectors of regional limestone-adapted plants.

planting.note: Divide mature rhizome clumps in spring and plant in moist, well-drained, neutral-to-acid soil in shade, sheltered from cold winter wind; named for its bold horizontal gold bands.

directions: Discovered on China's Mount Emei and introduced to cultivation in the mid-2000s, this striking selection carries long, arching, branched fronds banded with regular horizontal stripes of gold against deep green, giving the whole plant a bamboo-like look despite being a true fern. It spreads gradually from a rhizome into an increasingly dense, patch-forming clump rather than staying in a tight crown. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acid soil in shade, with shelter from harsh winter wind at the cooler end of its range. Its patterned foliage makes a strong focal point among plainer-leaved shade companions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil or on a slope or berm in dappled shade; this epiphytic species resents standing water around its roots.

directions: In its native forests of China, Taiwan, and Vietnam this fern grows as an epiphyte or lithophyte, its leathery, felt-surfaced fronds conserving moisture so effectively that established plants tolerate real dry spells. New fronds emerge pale green and darken with rusty undersides as they mature, creeping slowly outward on a shallow rhizome rather than forming a tidy single crown. Grow it on a sloped bed, berm, or well-drained pot of gritty, humus-rich soil in dappled shade, since good drainage matters more than steady moisture. Divide established plants to propagate, as its spores are notoriously slow to germinate.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in loose, sharply drained soil on a slope or in a container in shade; a Taiwanese species that resents sitting wet through winter.

directions: Named for its distinctively lobed, hand-shaped fronds, this Taiwanese felt fern unfurls new growth covered in fine silvery hairs that give it a star-dusted look before darkening with age. It is naturally slow and clumping, staying compact enough for years in a small pot, and tolerates container culture better than most ferns thanks to its drought-tolerant, felted foliage. Plant it in loose, fast-draining soil on a slope or in a container kept in shade, and move containers somewhere drier or warmer during extended wet or cold weather. It spreads by division or by slow-germinating spores shed in late winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a coarse, bark-based, well-drained epiphyte mix in bright indirect light to shade; grow as a container or houseplant outside zones 9-11.

directions: One of the most widely grown selections of the golden polypody, this cultivar is prized for broad, wavy-margined fronds in a distinctive blue-gray-green that sets it apart from the plain green species. In the wild it grows as an epiphyte on tree bark and rock, so it performs best in a loose, chunky, fast-draining mix rather than dense potting soil. Keep the creeping, fuzzy rhizomes partly exposed at the soil surface and water once the mix has dried slightly, since soggy roots cause more problems than underwatering. It tolerates lower light better than most ferns, making it an easygoing choice for a shaded patio or indoor spot alike.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in cool, moist, rich woodland soil in shade; this finely cut sport of the native oak fern spreads gently without becoming invasive.

directions: This plumose selection of the delicate native oak fern takes the species' already-dainty triangular fronds a step further, overlapping and ruffling the tiny leaflets into an almost feathery texture. Fronds emerge light green in spring, deepening to a soft blue-green through the growing season before dying back completely in fall. It spreads gradually by thin creeping rhizomes into a loose, low patch that is well mannered enough for edging a shaded path or tucking among rocks, never overwhelming neighboring plants. Give it consistently moist, rich, cool woodland soil in shade, since it struggles in hot, dry conditions or full sun.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity; grow as a container or hanging-basket houseplant outside zones 10-12.

directions: This selection of the popular delta maidenhair stands out for new fronds that emerge in warm bronze-red tones along dark, wiry stems before settling into a soft, airy green, with pinnules so finely cut that the overall effect reads almost cloud-like. It demands the same constant moisture and still, humid air as the species, browning quickly if the growing medium dries out, drafts hit it, or humidity drops too low. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in deep shade, and treat it as a hanging-basket or dish-garden houseplant everywhere outside the warmest, most sheltered zone 10-12 gardens. Divide and repot congested plants in spring as new growth resumes.
